background.definition: Infant botulism is a progressive, acute, symmetric, descending flaccid motor paralysis with prominent bulbar palsies caused by ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores.

list.listitem: 2.1 cases per 100,000 live births present annually in the United States.
Mean age at onset of symptoms is 14 weeks (median 12 weeks, range 0-52 weeks).
Ninety-five percent of infant botulism occurs in infants younger than 6 months.
Primarily Clostridium botulinum, and rarely Clostridium butyricum or Clostridium baratii.
Honey is associated with botulism (OR = 9.8).
In a study in California, only 10% of honey contained botulinum spores. Honey should not be given to an infant younger than 1 year.
In one case, an infant acquired infant botulism through application of "medicated honey" to an open wound.
The proportion of cases of infant botulism that included a history of honey exposure has decreased from 40% in the 1970s to 5% in the 2000s. In California, most infant botulism is from soil.
In a study in Argentina, 8% of chamomile tea contained botulinum spores.
In adults, cases of botulism have been reported following cosmetic botulinum toxin injections.
It has also been reported following ingestion of bootleg alcohol in prisons made from rotting potatoes ("pruno"), and wound infections from skin popping of black tar heroin.
When ingested, Clostridium botulinum spores colonize in the large intestine and produce botulinum toxin.
Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing symmetrical, descending generalized weakness, bulbar palsy, and constipation.
Advise parents not to give their infant honey or honey products before 1 year of age. B
Infant botulism is a clinical diagnosis; consider it in an infant with progressive generalized weakness, poor suck, weak cry, ophthalmoplegia, and constipation. C
While asking about honey exposure is important, most cases of infant botulism have no history of honey exposure. B
Definitive diagnosis is by isolating Clostridium botulinum toxin in stool. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Longer history of progressive weakness, no ophthalmoplegia, no constipation
Positive laboratory studies for metabolic disease

Differential.Differential_Name: Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
Differential.Differential_Features: Elevated CSF protein, demyelinating pattern on EMG

list.listitem: Suspect infant botulism in an infant (<1 year) with progressive generalized weakness (88%), lethargy (60%), weak cry (18%), poor suck/poor feeding (79%), bulbar palsy, and constipation (65%).
Take a careful history, including constipation, diet, and exposures. Constipation is often the first presenting symptom.

A careful neurologic examination should include examination for tone, weakness, ptosis (hold the patient’s head erect to examine for ptosis), dilated or sluggishly reactive pupils (examine in a dark room), fatigability, and suck.
Rarely, infant botulism may present catastrophically (eg, acute life-threatening event, cardiac arrest), which may delay diagnosis.
Definitive diagnosis of infant botulism is by isolating botulinum toxin from the stool.

Do not wait for spontaneous stool production as many infants have constipation. Obtain stool by gentle digital examination or enema with 5 to 30 mL of nonbacteriostatic water. Refer to www.infantbotulism.org for specific instructions.
A characteristic EMG pattern of brief-duration, small-amplitude, overly abundant motor-unit action potentials may be found in 86% of patients with infant botulism.
Suspect infant botulism in an infant (<1 year) with progressive generalized symmetrical weakness, weak cry, poor suck, bulbar palsy, and constipation.
Begin treatment with botulism immune globulin intravenous (human) (BIG-IV, or BabyBIG) while awaiting stool botulinum toxin results.

Treat with human origin botulism anti-A, anti-B immune globulin intravenous (BIG-IV, also known as BabyBIG) when infant botulism is suspected; it results in faster recovery compared with later treatment.B
Do not wait for laboratory confirmation of diagnosis prior to treatment. C
Provide supportive care with nasogastric feeding (needed in 95%) and/or mechanical ventilation (needed in up to 83%) as needed. C

Treat with human origin botulism anti-A, anti-B immune globulin intravenous (BIG-IV, also known as BabyBIG) when infant botulism is suspected; it results in faster recovery compared with later treatment.
The recommended dose of BabyBIG is 1.0 ml/kg (50 mg/kg) given as a single IV infusion as soon as botulism is clinically diagnosed (https://www.drugs.com/dosage/babybig.html).

In a small RCT of 122 infants hospitalized with botulism, infants were treated within 3 days of admission. Compared with placebo, those treated with BIG-IV or Baby-BIG had shorter hospital stays (2.6 vs 5.7 weeks) and had a reduction in intensive care by 3.2 weeks, mechanical ventilation by 2.6 weeks, and the need for IV or nasogastric feeding by 6.4 weeks.

An open-label study in 382 infants with botulism showed that BIG-IV within 3 days of hospitalization decreases duration of hospitalization by 1 week compared to treatment started later, on hospital days 4 to 7.

A 15-year safety review found that 1-5% of individuals who received botulism antitoxin experienced adverse events including hypersensitivity, pyrexia, tachycardia, bradycardia, anaphylaxis, and blood pressure increases.
Over 2/3 to 3/4 of patients with infant botulism require mechanical ventilation.
Virtually all infants (95%) require nasogastric tube feeding.
Hospitalize all patients with infant botulism for observation, supportive care (nasogastric tube feeding and/or ventilatory support as needed), and treatment with BIG-IV.
Rarely, infants with botulism may relapse within 2 weeks of complete resolution of symptoms, so close follow up is needed. B
No relapse has been reported after treatment with BIG-IV, which neutralizes botulinum toxin for at least 6 months. B
In the United States, 65% of botulism is infant botulism, 15% is food-borne, and 20% is wound-related.
Food-borne botulism occurs from eating food contaminated with botulinum toxin (often from eating home-canned food).

In food-borne botulism, crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting may precede neurologic symptoms. Afebrile, symmetric descending flaccid paralysis with prominent bulbar palsies, but clear sensorium, may occur anywhere from 2 hours to 8 days after exposure.
Wound botulism occurs when Clostridium botulinum infects a wound.
Treat food-borne botulism with equine botulinum antitoxin and supportive care.
